This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Lynda Kenyon.
President Trump is celebrating Johnson Wong's reinstatement as NVIDIA CEO, as well as his
part in the decision.
The two have been close allies, with Wong advising the president and also donating to
the White House Ballroom, NPR's Danielle Kurtzleben reports.
In a lengthy phone interview, Trump told CNBC Monday that he convinced NVIDIA to reinstate
Wong.
The president also said that he thinks he was successful because NVIDIA's stock price
plummeted after Wong's ouster.
Trump also posted an altered photo yesterday playing off the famous picture of him after
he was shot in Butler, Pennsylvania.
In this new picture, it's Wong, not Trump, raising his fist with blood spattered on his
face.
And in that fist is a red bra, referencing Wong's affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Wong is scheduled to publicly testify before the Senate Banking Committee in December.
Lawmakers from both parties have criticized Wong's reinstatement.
Danielle Kurtzleben and PR News.
Community is all along the California coast are preparing for potentially record high
tide levels this week.
Ezra David Romero of member station KQED has the latest.
The San Francisco Bay Area is bracing for three rounds of king tides this fall and winter.
The first is expected to peak 2.7 feet above normal because of elevated sea levels caused
by El Nino.
Daniel Swain is a climate scientist with the University of California system.
Nonetheless, we may still approach or exceed all time record water levels even without
a significant storm in the Bay Area.
He says this week's king tides will likely be the weakest of two other cycles around
Christmas and in January.
The region could see some rain midweek.
That's also when tides will peak before gradually falling on Thanksgiving Day.
For NPR News, I'm Ezra David Romero in San Francisco.
An Israeli medical charity says the expansion of military checkpoints in the occupied bank,
West Bank, is endangering lives.
Physicians for Human Rights Israel has published interviews with 25 Palestinian paramedics,
including one who says Israeli soldiers prevented him from reaching a wounded man nearby, leaving
him to bleed to death.
In a new report, the group cites a 350 percent spike in such incidents, including violence
directed at medical workers themselves between 2022 and 2024.
Imran Anati, the report's author, calls this collective punishment.
By blocking an ambulance to evacuate a patient, you're blocking the health care to the whole
Palestinian community.
One Palestinian mayor says six of his residents have died in ambulances delayed at checkpoints
over the past three years.
Asked about the report, the Israeli military told NPR it works to facilitate safe passage
of medical teams subject to security assessment.
Lauren Fryer, NPR News, Tel Aviv.
You're listening to NPR News.
A mathematician at the A.I. firm Anthropic, says the company's chatbot, has solved another
one of the toughest problems in the field.
NPR's Jeff Brumfield reports other experts think the solution could be correct.
The Riemann hypothesis has to do with the distribution of prime numbers.
On Friday, a mathematician at Anthropic said he'd use the company's Claude to prove the
hypothesis was correct.
Claude provided its proof in the form of computer code that can be checked by other computers.
The problem is that proof is 17 million lines long.
Still, the computer check says it's right and Andrew Sutherland of MIT believes it.
Even though I have no understanding of the proof, and nobody does, I am more confident
that this proof is correct than any proof I have ever encountered.
It may be a while before mathematicians can verify this result, especially since they
have hundreds of other A.I. solutions they still need to check.
Jeff Brumfield, NPR News.
The Vatican is releasing excerpts of Pope Francis' private diary.
In it, the late Pope wrote that he saw the gates of hell when he realized the depths
of the clergy sexual abuse scandal.
The diary also reveals that the Argentine Pope suffered a profound spiritual crisis
in 2021 and 2022 that was connected to his own temptations, he wrote, to exercise power
omnipotently.
The diary is called The Private Diary of Pope Francis.
It is being published in several languages around the world starting today.
I'm Linda Kenyon, NPR News, in Washington.
